\begin{abstract}Dealers set limits on the largest position reached before a review horizon ends. We compare conditional quantile forecasts with historical rules using hourly FX, daily aggregates and weekly dealer positions. Simple historical rules are hard to beat. Long-history FX regression lowers matched loss by 14.8\% and 16.6\% across periods. Delayed calibration retains the later gain (15.0\%), with 329 versus 328 breaches. Rankings against a shorter rolling rule vary by period. Expanded regularization leaves regression behind in 34 of 48 weekly panel comparisons, and historical rules win most daily comparisons. Stationary controlled simulations already produce large short-history losses. In newly calibrated simulations, loss rises by 116.2\% under constant parameters and 121.4\% under parameter switching. The full longer-history summaries are unavailable. The mechanism behind the observed low-frequency losses remains unidentified. Peak-limit validation should assess accuracy, breaches and reference stability together.\end{abstract}

contexts.context_exact: \refstepcounter{proposition}\noindent\textbf{Proposition~\theproposition (known-floor projection).}\label{prop:floor} Suppose \(Y\ge B\) almost surely and the issue information contains \(B\). Projecting any forecast \(c\) to \(\max\{B,c\}\) weakly improves pinball loss for every possible outcome, with an exact gain below the floor. If \(q\) is the true conditional lower inverse quantile at level \(1-\alpha\), its strict exceedance probability is at most \(\alpha\). At an atom of the response distribution, that probability can be smaller than the nominal tail probability.
\rho_\tau(Y-c)-\rho_\tau(Y-\max\{B,c\})=\tau(B-c)_+,\qquad \Pr(Y>q\mid\mathcal F_t)\le\alpha.

\refstepcounter{proposition}\noindent\textbf{Proposition~\theproposition (classical endpoint-to-peak bound).}\label{prop:levy} Let future increments be independent and individually symmetric about zero, with partial sums \(S_h\). Fix a starting position \(x\), set \(B=|x|\), and let \(q\) be the population \((1-\alpha/2)\) quantile of \(|S_H|\). The triangle inequality and the classical scalar L\'evy maximal inequality then imply the following bound, including strict inequalities at atoms \citep{sussman2023}. Neither identical increment distributions nor finite increment moments are required for this population statement.
\Pr\!\left(\max_{0\le h\le H}|x+S_h|>B+q\right)\le\Pr\!\left(\max_h|S_h|>q\right)\le2\Pr(|S_H|>q)\le\alpha.

Separately fitted horizon forecasts can violate the ordering of true peak quantiles. Short-history FX regression crosses across horizons on 640 evaluation origins. Label nesting, floor coverage and strict-breach definitions provide additional checks on the issued reports.

The FX application uses the hourly Net Position Time Series Dataset, reporting market-maker client-flow positions \citep{dataset,wisniewski2020}. It contains 18,576 records in source USD units. The later, earlier and full-prefix comparisons use distinct chronological issue grids and the same sampled-peak definition.

The weekly data are New York Fed Primary Dealer Statistics \citep{nyfeddata}. Reporting definitions follow the government-securities dealer framework and position-accounting instructions \citep{fr2004_2013,fr2004_2024}. The Treasury-bill series has 706 economic-date observations in USD millions. The values are fair-value positions aggregated as long-minus-short totals. Additional categories pass metadata and calendar checks and use complete weekly grids, with separate fits by category.

Daily aggregation takes the last recorded position on each nonempty source-naive calendar day. It retains partial boundary days, yielding 930 days and 501 common evaluation issues. Reports use the completed day's end as their issue clock. The resulting target is a peak over subsequent daily records.

Forecasts target the conditional quantile at \(\tau=19/20\). The horizons \(H\in\{6,24\}\) count subsequent source records, and each peak includes the issue position. Calendar gaps extend an FX horizon's elapsed span; weekly and daily steps represent different review intervals. The nineteen-to-one error-weight preference defines the evaluation score.
notes: 19/20 = .95; underprediction / unused weight = .95/.05 =19:1. Constants are fixed evaluation preferences, not estimated funding costs.

contexts.context_exact: The earlier FX ranking reverses when the reference changes. Against shorter-history rolling headroom, later loss falls by 12.7\%, but earlier loss rises by 3.2\%. Matched gains and rolling-reference gains therefore have different period stability (Table~\ref{tab:fx}).

Short-history FX regression performs poorly at the longer horizon. Loss rises by 31.5\% against matched historical headroom. Regression records 924 breaches against 427 for the reference; the full horizon map retains the other adverse comparisons.

Treasury-bill regression loses on both accuracy and breaches. Mean loss rises by 50.8\%, with 54 regression breaches. Historical headroom records 28 breaches; the earlier short-window version also loses (Table~\ref{tab:weekly}).

Stronger regularization narrows weekly panel losses but leaves historical rules ahead. Median excess loss falls from 92.6\% to 9.2\% after menu expansion. Regression still loses 34 of 48 matched comparisons. Conservative selection leaves a worst-cell increase of 181.4\% in the earlier weekly grid. This is the Treasury-bill short-window, 24-step comparison (Table~\ref{tab:weekly}).

Simpler conditional reports and fixed combinations also give mixed weekly results. The median combination lowers Treasury-bill loss by 4.0\%, while the mean combination raises it by 2.8\%. The headroom recursion is also worse. The Supplement retains every completed loss and model failure.

Historical headroom wins seven of eight same-record daily comparisons. The exception uses four predictors, history 260 and horizon 6, reducing loss by 3.0\%. It records 37 breaches versus 30 for matched headroom. Daily aggregation therefore preserves the score--breach disagreement while changing the leading forecast in most comparisons.

contexts.context_exact: The new experiment calibrates constant and segmented AR--GARCH--t processes to pre-evaluation prefixes of thirteen weekly series. The joint OLS score uses Hansen's statistic \citep{hansen1992}. A fitted constant-parameter null supplies its parametric bootstrap reference. Seven series reject at the pointwise 5\% level; Holm adjustment retains two. A constrained descriptive partition selects up to two changes. The switching arm cycles the fitted regimes; its constant counterpart retains the whole-prefix parameters. The arms transform common uniforms through their own innovation laws and use the controlled grid's forecasting procedures.

contexts.context_exact: The daily fitted null fails the fourth-moment qualification, and the matched-calendar hourly null fails optimization. Their requested diagnostic comparison is also unassessable. The observed weekly rejection count supports the registered screening threshold, while the remaining results leave the proposed explanation unresolved. Instability is not necessary for large losses in these simulated procedures: the fitted constant controls already generate them. The evidence leaves the empirical low-frequency mechanism unidentified.

contexts.context_exact: Simple historical rules are hard to beat for peak net positions. Hourly FX regression lowers matched loss by 14.8\% and 16.6\% across periods. Delayed calibration retains the later gain with 329 versus 328 breaches. Rankings against the shorter rolling reference change by period.

Weekly regression still loses 34 of 48 expanded-panel comparisons, and historical headroom wins most same-record daily comparisons. Conservative validation leaves substantial losses. Stationary controlled and fitted constant-parameter processes also produce large short-history losses. The switching experiment leaves the low-frequency mechanism unidentified, with required longer-history results incomplete. Peak-limit validation should compare accuracy, error amounts, breaches and reference stability together.

\paragraph{Data availability.} The FX input is the specified version of the Kaggle Net Position Time Series Dataset. The owning metadata labels its license ``Data files \copyright\ Original Authors.'' This repository supplies the acquisition route and input fingerprint, but excludes raw FX observations and private per-issue prediction vectors. Obtain the source from \url{https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/davidlindsay1979/net-position-time-series-dataset} subject to the original rights holders' terms.

\paragraph{Code availability.} Code, saved results and version-specific reproduction instructions are available at \url{https://github.com/ByronLi0207/financial-mathematics-paper-20261020/tree/revision-v9}. The package includes all earlier comparisons, calibrated simulations and the new stability study. Document compilation and restricted-input financial replay have separate instructions. Complete, adverse, failed and unavailable outcomes are retained.

S091.raw_value: Let the forecast-origin information include B, let Y≥B almost surely, and let 0<τ<1. Project any issued report c to max(B,c). Its pinball loss is no larger at every possible Y. A true conditional lower inverse quantile q at level τ=1−α has strict breach probability at most α. Equality is not automatic: an atom at the quantile can make the probability smaller. The lower bound alone need not create an outcome atom; fitted reports do not inherit the population statement.

S093.raw_value: Let future real increments be independent and individually symmetric about zero. Write S<sub>h</sub> for their partial sums, S<sub>0</sub>=0, and fix an observed starting position x with B=|x|. No identical-distribution or finite-moment assumption is required. If q is the population (1−α/2) quantile of |S<sub>H</sub>|, the report B+q has strict peak-breach probability at most α. This is a direct scalar application of the classical Lévy maximal inequality, not a new inequality.
